claim: Antimicrobial resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is one of the greatest threats to global health.
source: Antimicrobial resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is one of the greatest threats to global health.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the severity of antimicrobial resistance.

claim: Most available adjuvants are only effective against specific resistance proteins.
source: Most available adjuvants are only effective against specific resistance proteins.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the limitations of current antibiotic adjuvants.

claim: Impairing DsbA-mediated disulfide bond formation incapacitates diverse β-lactamases.
source: In particular, we find that impairing DsbA-mediated disulfide bond formation incapacitates diverse β-lactamases and destabilizes mobile colistin resistance enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reduced MIC values for β-lactamases in dsbA mutants.

claim: Impairing DsbA-mediated disulfide bond formation destabilizes mobile colistin resistance enzymes.
source: In particular, we find that impairing DsbA-mediated disulfide bond formation incapacitates diverse β-lactamases and destabilizes mobile colistin resistance enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced MCR protein levels and colistin MIC values in dsbA mutants.

claim: Chemical inhibition of DsbA sensitizes multidrug-resistant clinical isolates to existing antibiotics.
source: Furthermore, we show that chemical inhibition of DsbA sensitizes multidrug-resistant clinical isolates to existing antibiotics and that the absence of DsbA, in combination with antibiotic treatment, substantially increases the survival of Galleria mellonella larvae infected with multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data from clinical isolates treated with DsbB inhibitor.

claim: The absence of DsbA, in combination with antibiotic treatment, substantially increases the survival of Galleria mellonella larvae infected with multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Furthermore, we show that chemical inhibition of DsbA sensitizes multidrug-resistant clinical isolates to existing antibiotics and that the absence of DsbA, in combination with antibiotic treatment, substantially increases the survival of Galleria mellonella larvae infected with multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from G. mellonella infection experiments.

claim: More than 6500 unique enzymes capable of degrading β-lactam compounds have been identified to date.
source: More than 6500 unique enzymes capable of degrading β-lactam compounds have been identified to date (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by reference to supplementary data.

claim: β-lactams are the most commonly prescribed antibiotics worldwide.
source: This constant emergence of resistance not only threatens β-lactams, the most commonly prescribed antibiotics worldwide (Meletis, 2016; Versporten et al., 2018), but also increases the use of last-resort agents, like the polymyxin antibiotic colistin, for the treatment of multidrug-resistant infections (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Since their discovery in 2015, 10 families of MCR proteins have been identified.
source: Since their discovery in 2015, 10 families of MCR proteins have been identified and these enzymes are quickly becoming a major threat to the longevity of colistin (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: DsbA assists the folding of hundreds of proteins in the periplasm.
source: DsbA has been shown to assist the folding of hundreds of proteins in the periplasm (Kadokura et al., 2004; Dutton et al., 2008; Vertommen et al., 2008; Figure 1A), including a vast range of virulence factors (Heras et al., 2009; Landeta et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The absence of DsbA resulted in a substantial decrease in MIC values (> 2 fold cutoff) for all but one of the tested β-lactamases.
source: We found that the absence of DsbA resulted in a substantial decrease in MIC values ( > 2 fold cutoff) for all but one of the tested β-lactamases (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data shown in figures.

claim: For SHV-27, the lack of DsbA resulted in a noticeable drop in the cefuroxime MIC value under temperature stress conditions (at 43 °C rather than 37 °C).
source: For the β-lactamase that seemed unaffected by the absence of DsbA, SHV-27, we performed the same experiment under temperature stress conditions (at 43 °C rather than 37 °C). Under these conditions, the lack of DsbA also resulted in a noticeable drop in the cefuroxime MIC value (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of MCR enzymes in E. coli K-12 strain resulted in colistin resistance (MIC of 3 μg/mL or higher).
source: Expression of MCR enzymes in our wild-type E. coli K-12 strain resulted in colistin resistance (MIC of 3 μg/mL or higher), while the strain harboring the empty vector was sensitive to colistin (MIC of 1 μg/mL).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data.

claim: The absence of DsbA caused re-sensitization of MCR-expressing strains to colistin, as defined by the EUCAST breakpoint.
source: In almost all tested cases, the absence of DsbA caused re-sensitization of the strains, as defined by the EUCAST breakpoint (E. coli strains with an MIC of 2 μg/mL or below are classified as susceptible; Figure 1C), indicating that DsbA is important for MCR function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type MIC values could be restored for all tested cysteine-containing enzymes by complementation of dsbA.
source: Wild-type MIC values could be restored for all tested cysteine-containing enzymes by complementation of dsbA (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation experiments shown in supplementary figures.

claim: No decreases in MIC values for the aminoglycoside antibiotic gentamicin were observed in dsbA mutants expressing β-lactamases.
source: We observed no decreases in MIC values for the aminoglycoside antibiotic gentamicin, which is not affected by the activity of the tested enzymes (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data shown in figures.

claim: The cell envelope integrity of the dsbA mutant is comparable to the parental strain.
source: All four assays confirmed that the cell envelope integrity of the dsbA mutant is comparable to the parental strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NPN, vancomycin, PI, and CPRG assays.

claim: MIC values for the dsbA mutant were lower than for the parental strain for all tested RND efflux pump substrate antibiotics.
source: MIC values for the dsbA mutant were lower than for the parental strain for all tested substrate antibiotics, but remained unchanged for the non-substrate gentamicin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The MIC drop for chloramphenicol caused by deletion of dsbA sensitized the E. coli MG1655 dsbA strain to chloramphenicol.
source: It is notable that the MIC drop for this pump substrate, caused by deletion of dsbA, sensitized the E. coli MG1655 dsbA strain to chloramphenicol (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MIC data shown in Figure 1D and comparison to EUCAST breakpoint.

claim: All Ambler class A and B β-lactamases, except GES-1, exhibited drastically reduced protein levels when expressed in the dsbA mutant.
source: When expressed in the dsbA mutant, all Ambler class A and B β-lactamases (Table 1), except GES-1 which we were not able to visualize by immunoblotting, exhibited drastically reduced protein levels whilst the amount of the control enzyme L2-1 remained unaffected (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No decrease in protein amounts for Ambler class D enzymes was detected in the dsbA mutant.
source: We did not detect any decrease in protein amounts for Ambler class D enzymes (Table 1, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The hydrolytic activity of Ambler class D β-lactamases was significantly lower in the dsbA mutant.
source: However, the hydrolytic activity of these β-lactamases was significantly lower in the dsbA mutant (Figure 2C), suggesting a folding defect that leads to loss of function.
evidence: This claim is supported by nitrocefin hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MCR enzymes were undetectable when expressed in a dsbA mutant.
source: Like with class A and B β-lactamases, MCR enzymes were undetectable when expressed in a dsbA mutant (Figure 3A) suggesting that their stability or folding is severely compromised when they lack their disulfide bonds.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For dsbA mutants expressing MCR-3, –5, and –8, the peaks at m/z 1821.2 and m/z 1919.2 could no longer be detected by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry.
source: For dsbA mutants expressing MCR-3, –5, and –8 (Figure 3C), the peaks at m/z 1821.2 and m/z 1919.2 could no longer be detected, whilst the native lipid A peak at m/z 1796.2 remained unchanged (Figure 3B, fourth spectrum); dsbA mutants expressing MCR-4 retain some basal lipid A-modifying activity, nonetheless this is not sufficient for this strain to efficiently evade colistin treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: In the absence of DsbA, degradation of DegP occurred, reducing the pool of active enzyme.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, we found that in the absence of DsbA degradation of DegP occurred (Figure 4A), reducing the pool of active enzyme (Skórko-Glonek et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and citation to published literature.

claim: AcrA accumulated to the same extent in a dsbA and a degP mutant.
source: In addition, AcrA accumulated to the same extent in a dsbA and a degP mutant (Figure 4B), suggesting that in both these strains AcrA was not efficiently cleared.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No accumulation was detected for the outer-membrane protein TolC in dsbA or degP mutants.
source: Finally, no accumulation was detected for the outer-membrane protein TolC (Figure 4C), which is not a DegP substrate (Werner et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C and citation to published literature.

claim: Chemical inhibition of the DSB system impedes flagellar motility in E. coli MC1000.
source: We first tested the motility of E. coli MC1000 in the presence of the inhibitor and found that cells were significantly less motile (Figure 5AB), consistent with the fact that impairing DSB function prevents the formation of the flagellar P-ring component FlgI (Dailey and Berg, 1993; Hizukuri et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B, and citations to published literature.

claim: Addition of the DsbB inhibitor to growing E. coli MC1000 cells resulted in accumulation of inactive reduced DsbA.
source: By contrast, addition of the inhibitor to growing E. coli MC1000 cells resulted in accumulation of inactive reduced DsbA, thus confirming that DsbB function was impeded (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AMS labeling data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Addition of the DsbB inhibitor during MIC testing phenocopied the effects of a dsbA deletion on β-lactamase and MCR activity.
source: We determined MIC values for the latest generation β-lactam that each β-lactamase can hydrolyze, or colistin, for our panel of E. coli MC1000 strains and found that addition of the compound during MIC testing phenocopied the effects of a dsbA deletion on β-lactamase and MCR activity (Figure 5DE, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Addition of the DsbB inhibitor does not affect the growth profile of E. coli MC1000.
source: The observed effects are not a result of altered cell growth, as addition of the compound does not affect the growth profile of the bacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), in agreement with the fact that deletion of dsbA does not affect cell viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DSB system inhibition in a clinical isolate of K. pneumoniae expressing KPC-2 sensitized the strain to imipenem as defined by EUCAST breakpoints.
source: DSB system inhibition in a clinical isolate of K. pneumoniae expressing KPC-2 sensitized the strain to imipenem as defined by EUCAST breakpoints (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The combination of the DSB system inhibitor with imipenem led to dramatic changes in the appearance of K. pneumoniae cells, whose integrity was entirely compromised.
source: By contrast, the combination of the inhibitor with imipenem (added at a sub-MIC final concentration of 6 µg/mL), led to dramatic changes in the appearance of the cells, whose integrity was entirely compromised (Figure 6B, bottom row).
evidence: This claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 6B.

claim: E. coli and Citrobacter freundii isolates expressing KPC-2 showed clinically relevant decreases in their MIC values for imipenem when their DSB system was chemically inhibited.
source: Similarly, E. coli and Citrobacter freundii isolates expressing KPC-2, including multidrug-resistant strains, also showed clinically relevant decreases in their MIC values for imipenem that resulted in sensitization when their DSB system was chemically inhibited (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For an E. cloacae isolate expressing FRI-1, chemical inhibition of DsbA caused reduction in its aztreonam MIC value by over 180 µg/mL, resulting in intermediate resistance as defined by EUCAST breakpoints.
source: For an E. cloacae isolate expressing FRI-1, chemical inhibition of DsbA caused reduction in its aztreonam MIC value by over 180 µg/mL, resulting in intermediate resistance as defined by EUCAST breakpoints (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Combination of the DSB system inhibitor with colistin led to reduction of the colistin MIC and sensitization of MCR-1-expressing multidrug-resistant E. coli.
source: We found that combination of the DSB system inhibitor with colistin led to reduction of the colistin MIC and sensitization of MCR-1-expressing multidrug-resistant E. coli (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SEM images of MCR-1-expressing E. coli after combination treatment using sub-MIC amounts of colistin revealed drastic changes in morphology, whereby cells blebbed intensely or their contents leaked out.
source: In agreement with this, SEM images of this strain after combination treatment using sub-MIC amounts of colistin (final concentration of 2 µg/mL) revealed drastic changes in morphology, whereby cells blebbed intensely or their contents leaked out (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 7B.

claim: DSB system inhibition allowed sensitization to colistin for eight additional clinical E. coli isolates that encode diverse MCR enzymes.
source: We tested eight additional clinical E. coli isolates that encode diverse MCR enzymes (most of which are multidrug resistant) and have colistin MICs ranging from 3 to 16 µg/mL; DSB system inhibition also allowed sensitization to colistin (Figure 7C) for tested strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: DSB system inhibition in E. coli CNR1790 led to a decrease in its ceftazidime MIC, resulting in intermediate resistance.
source: At the same time, we were able to show that DSB system inhibition in E. coli CNR1790 (i.e. the clinical isolate expressing both MCR-1 and the ESBL TEM-15 that was sensitized to colistin in Figure 7A), led to a decrease in its ceftazidime MIC, resulting in intermediate resistance (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Deletion of dsbA1 in a multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa clinical isolate expressing OXA-198 led to sensitization of this strain to the antipseudomonal β-lactam piperacillin.
source: Nonetheless, deletion of dsbA1 in a multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa clinical isolate expressing OXA-198 (PA43417), led to sensitization of this strain to the antipseudomonal β-lactam piperacillin (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Deletion of dsbA1 in P. aeruginosa PAe191 caused a drastic reduction in the ceftazidime MIC value by over 220 µg/mL, and sensitized the strain to aztreonam.
source: In this case, absence of DsbA caused a drastic reduction in the ceftazidime MIC value by over 220 µg/mL, and sensitized the strain to aztreonam (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MIC data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Treatment of larvae infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 dsbA1 with 7.5 µg/mL ceftazidime resulted in 83% survival, 50 hr post infection.
source: Treatment of larvae infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 dsbA1 with 7.5 µg/mL ceftazidime (pink curve) results in 83% survival, 50 hr post infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by Galleria mellonella survival assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: 100% of the G. mellonella larvae infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 die 18 hr post infection.
source: 100% of the G. mellonella larvae infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 (blue curve) or infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 and treated with 7.5 µg/mL ceftazidime (red curve) die 18 hr post infection, and only 20% of the larvae infected with P. aeruginosa PAe191 dsbA1 (light blue curve) survive 50 hr post infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by Galleria mellonella survival assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: DsbA introduces disulfide bonds into extracytoplasmic proteins containing two or more cysteine residues.
source: DsbA introduces disulfide bonds into extracytoplasmic proteins containing two or more cysteine residues.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about DsbA function and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: After each round of oxidative protein folding, DsbA is regenerated by the quinone (Q)-containing protein DsbB.
source: After each round of oxidative protein folding, DsbA is regenerated by the quinone (Q)-containing protein DsbB, which in turn transfers the reducing equivalents to the respiratory chain (RC) (Kadokura et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: DsbA dependence is conserved within phylogenetic groups of β-lactamases.
source: DsbA dependence is conserved within phylogenetic groups (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Based on the number of enzymes belonging to the same phylogenetic family as the β-lactamases tested in this study, a total of 195 discrete enzymes are anticipated to rely on DsbA for their stability and function.
source: As DsbA dependence is conserved within phylogenetic groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), based on the number of enzymes belonging to the same phylogenetic family as the β-lactamases tested in this study (Supplementary file 1), we anticipate that a total of 195 discrete enzymes rely on DsbA for their stability and function, 84 of which cannot be inhibited by classical adjuvant approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: 84 of the 195 discrete enzymes anticipated to rely on DsbA cannot be inhibited by classical adjuvant approaches.
source: As DsbA dependence is conserved within phylogenetic groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), based on the number of enzymes belonging to the same phylogenetic family as the β-lactamases tested in this study (Supplementary file 1), we anticipate that a total of 195 discrete enzymes rely on DsbA for their stability and function, 84 of which cannot be inhibited by classical adjuvant approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: Approximately 56% of the β-lactamase phylogenetic families found in pathogens and organisms capable of causing opportunistic infections contain enzymes with two or more cysteines.
source: As such, together with the fact that approximately 56% of the β-lactamase phylogenetic families found in pathogens and organisms capable of causing opportunistic infections contain enzymes with two or more cysteines (Supplementary file 1), we expect many more clinically relevant β-lactamases, beyond those already tested in this study, to depend on DsbA.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to supplementary data.

claim: All MCR members contain multiple disulfide bonds.
source: As all MCR members contain multiple disulfide bonds, inhibition of the DSB system provides a broadly applicable solution for reversing MCR-mediated colistin resistance (Figures 1C, 5E and 7ABC) that would likely extend to novel MCR proteins that may emerge in the future.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about MCR protein structure.

claim: Absence of DsbA results in degradation of MCR enzymes and abrogation of their function.
source: Nonetheless, our findings in this study clearly demonstrate that absence of DsbA results in degradation of MCR enzymes and abrogation of their function (Figure 3), which, in turn, leads to sensitization of all tested E. coli clinical isolates to colistin (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: The cell envelope contains multiple protein folding catalysts.
source: Since the cell envelope contains multiple protein folding catalysts (Goemans et al., 2014), it would be worth testing if other redox proteins, chaperones, or proteases could be targeted to indirectly compromise efflux pumps.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The DSB system is essential for virulence.
source: In addition to assisting the folding of 40% of the cell-envelope proteome (Dutton et al., 2008; Vertommen et al., 2008), the DSB system is essential for virulence (Heras et al., 2009; Landeta et al., 2018), has a key role in the formation and awakening of bacterial persister cells (Wilmaerts et al., 2019) and, as seen in this work, is required for bacterial survival in the presence of widely used antibiotic compounds.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The DSB system has a key role in the formation and awakening of bacterial persister cells.
source: In addition to assisting the folding of 40% of the cell-envelope proteome (Dutton et al., 2008; Vertommen et al., 2008), the DSB system is essential for virulence (Heras et al., 2009; Landeta et al., 2018), has a key role in the formation and awakening of bacterial persister cells (Wilmaerts et al., 2019) and, as seen in this work, is required for bacterial survival in the presence of widely used antibiotic compounds.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The DSB system is required for bacterial survival in the presence of widely used antibiotic compounds.
source: In addition to assisting the folding of 40% of the cell-envelope proteome (Dutton et al., 2008; Vertommen et al., 2008), the DSB system is essential for virulence (Heras et al., 2009; Landeta et al., 2018), has a key role in the formation and awakening of bacterial persister cells (Wilmaerts et al., 2019) and, as seen in this work, is required for bacterial survival in the presence of widely used antibiotic compounds.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DSB system assists the folding of 40% of the cell-envelope proteome.
source: In addition to assisting the folding of 40% of the cell-envelope proteome (Dutton et al., 2008; Vertommen et al., 2008), the DSB system is essential for virulence (Heras et al., 2009; Landeta et al., 2018), has a key role in the formation and awakening of bacterial persister cells (Wilmaerts et al., 2019) and, as seen in this work, is required for bacterial survival in the presence of widely used antibiotic compounds.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Targeting the DSB system in Gram-negative pathogens could lead to adjuvant approaches that inactivate AMR determinants whilst simultaneously incapacitating an arsenal of virulence factors.
source: As shown in our in vivo experiments (Figure 8C), targeting such a system in Gram-negative pathogens could lead to adjuvant approaches that inactivate AMR determinants whilst simultaneously incapacitating an arsenal of virulence factors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on experimental data and inference.
